checkpoints.title: Integrate small changes and test immediately
checkpoints.prompt: Immediately after the development team registers a change, the automated tests for the order API fail. Select one action that should be taken as part of the continuous integration process.

choices.text: Stop distribution to the next environment and rerun the same tests after making the fix
choices.explanation: Stop the failure early and validate the fix.

choices.text: Ignore the failure and distribute to production
choices.explanation: This conflicts with the purpose of CI.

choices.text: Delete the tests
choices.explanation: Defects can no longer be detected.

learning.reason: A CI failure stops the subsequent stages.

checkpoints.title: Distinguish continuous delivery from continuous deployment
checkpoints.prompt: The operations team keeps tested changes in a state where they can be released at any time and applies them to production only when the responsible person approves them. Select one option that matches this policy.

choices.text: Continuous deployment
choices.explanation: This method automatically distributes changes to production without human approval.

choices.text: Continuous delivery
choices.explanation: It maintains a state in which changes can be released at any time.

choices.text: Manual rebuild
choices.explanation: This is not a definition of a distributable state.

checkpoints.title: Deliver verified artifacts directly to production
checkpoints.prompt: A release manager deploys the distribution artifact for an order API that passed testing in the verification environment to production. Select one way to use the verified artifact in production.

choices.text: Rebuild in production
choices.explanation: This can create differences from the artifact that was tested.

choices.text: Refer only to the “latest” tag
choices.explanation: The actual artifact cannot be fixed.

choices.text: Distribute the artifact with the same digest or version to the next environment
choices.explanation: This ensures that the artifact tested and the artifact distributed are the same.

learning.reason: Promote the same artifact between environments.

checkpoints.title: Defining conditions for proceeding to the next stage
checkpoints.prompt: The release manager confirmed that the required tests in the validation environment did not meet the passing criteria. Select one action to take next.

choices.text: Stop deployment to the next environment, keep the known-good version, and investigate the cause.
choices.explanation: A quality gate is a stopping condition that prevents artifacts that do not meet the requirements from proceeding to later stages.

choices.text: Continue deployment to production because it is the scheduled time.
choices.explanation: This ignores the unmet conditions.

choices.text: Lower the criteria without keeping an audit trail.
choices.explanation: This is not a reproducible operation.

learning.reason: If the quality gate is not met, stop and investigate.

choices.text: Incorporate commits and automatically run builds and tests to inspect changes quickly.
choices.explanation: CI uses commits as the starting point for builds and tests, detecting failures at an early stage.

choices.text: Once CI succeeds, production safety is guaranteed unconditionally.
choices.explanation: CI success means that the specified checks succeeded; it does not guarantee against all production risks.

choices.text: Check only whether the build succeeds, and run tests after deployment to production.
choices.explanation: CI requires running builds and tests so that failures are not passed to later stages.

finalQuestions.prompt: The development team wants to inspect changes quickly immediately after receiving a commit for the order API. Choose one correct description of continuous integration (CI).
finalQuestions.title: The Role of CI

choices.text: Run the same build and tests for each small commit.
choices.explanation: The shorter the distance between a change and its test results, the easier it is to trace the cause.

choices.text: When a failure occurs, check the logs, inputs, and changes, then rerun the same checks after making a fix.
choices.explanation: This is the correct approach: do not pass the failure to later stages, and verify it under the same conditions.

choices.text: Do not retain failure logs; combine several weeks of changes and then inspect them manually.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The differences become larger and the basis for the fix is lost, making it impossible to narrow down the cause.

finalQuestions.prompt: The development team that changed the order API wants to narrow down the cause of a failure during integration. Choose one incorrect approach.
finalQuestions.title: Tracing the Cause of Integration Failures

choices.text: Because CI succeeded, deploy to production without checking the monitoring plan or the next quality gate.
choices.explanation: CI success alone does not guarantee production safety; the next deployment conditions must be evaluated.

choices.text: Evaluate the next quality gate and deployment conditions for the candidate that passed the defined checks.
choices.explanation: CI results are test evidence used for downstream decisions.

choices.text: Discard the test results and manually rebuild from the same source for production.
choices.explanation: This breaks the correspondence with the test results and could change the artifact being deployed.

choices.text: Do not allow failed checks to proceed downstream; review the logs and changes, fix the issue, and rerun the checks.
choices.explanation: This stops failures early and verifies the fix using the same checks.

finalQuestions.prompt: The release manager uses the CI results for the order API to decide whether to deploy it to the next environment. Choose two appropriate actions.
finalQuestions.title: Using CI Results

choices.text: Continuous delivery keeps tested changes in a state where they can be released at any time.
choices.explanation: This is the correct description of delivery.

choices.text: Continuous delivery is a method that always deploys automatically to production without human approval.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Automatic deployment to production without human approval is continuous deployment.

choices.text: Continuous deployment is a method that automatically deploys changes that have passed the defined quality gates all the way to production.
choices.explanation: This is the correct description of deployment.

choices.text: Manual approval is not a substitute for testing; it can serve as a decision point for reviewing impact and monitoring.
choices.explanation: This correctly describes the role of approval in the prompt.

choices.text: If manual approval is added, builds and tests do not need to be run.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Approval is not a substitute for automated checks.

finalQuestions.prompt: The release engineer chooses how to deploy the order API from the test environment to production. Choose two incorrect statements about continuous delivery and continuous deployment.
finalQuestions.title: delivery and deployment

choices.text: Make automated tests unnecessary and proceed based only on the approver’s impression.
choices.explanation: Manual approval is not a substitute for automated tests.

choices.text: Review the change impact, change window, and monitoring plan before deciding whether to proceed.
choices.explanation: Manual approval can be used as a responsible decision point before deployment.

choices.text: Rebuild a production-specific artifact after approval.
choices.explanation: This is not the purpose of approval because it creates a difference from the tested artifact.

finalQuestions.prompt: The release manager deploys a tested web application from the test environment to production. Choose one appropriate use of manual approval.
finalQuestions.title: Pre-Production Approval

choices.text: This method is continuous deployment, which automatically deploys changes that have passed the defined quality gates.
choices.explanation: A method that automatically deploys to production without human approval is continuous deployment.

choices.text: Because it is continuous delivery, it is always automatically deployed to production without human approval.
choices.explanation: Delivery means that the release is in a releasable state; it does not necessarily mean automatic deployment to production.

choices.text: Because automatic deployment was selected, proceed to the next stage without recording quality-gate failures.
choices.explanation: Even with automatic deployment, the next stage must be stopped when the quality gate is not met.

choices.text: Verify by identifier that the artifact deployed to production is the same as the artifact tested in the validation environment.
choices.explanation: Regardless of the deployment method, the tested artifact and the deployed artifact can be traced.

choices.text: Rebuild a production artifact for each environmental difference, then deploy it automatically.
choices.explanation: Rebuilding creates a difference from the tested artifact.

finalQuestions.prompt: The payments team automatically deploys tested artifacts all the way to production without human approval. Select two correct actions according to the passage.
finalQuestions.title: Choosing a deployment method

choices.text: An artifact is a deployable unit, such as a package or container image generated by a build.
choices.explanation: This is the correct definition of an artifact described in the passage.

choices.text: Identifying an artifact by its digest or version makes it possible to track the deployed artifact.
choices.explanation: A version or digest is a correct identifier for specifying an artifact.

choices.text: Even if artifacts are rebuilt for each environment, the tested artifact and the deployed artifact are always identical as long as the source commit is the same.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Rebuilding can cause the artifact tested and the artifact deployed to production to differ.

finalQuestions.prompt: A release manager deploys to production a container image verified in the validation environment. Select one incorrect statement about artifacts.
finalQuestions.title: How to track artifacts

choices.text: Use only the release manager’s memory as the evidence linking the artifacts to the tests.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It is not reproducible evidence.

choices.text: Save the source commit, the artifact version or digest, and the test results.
choices.explanation: This is the correct action for associating the change, deployed artifact, and test results.

choices.text: Use the digest tested in the validation environment for the production deployment as well.
choices.explanation: This is the correct action for keeping the tested artifact and the deployed artifact identical.

choices.text: Record a production artifact rebuilt for production as if it were the same as the tested artifact.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The rebuilt artifact may differ from the tested artifact.

choices.text: Provide environment-specific endpoints as external configuration and do not change the artifact itself.
choices.explanation: This is the correct action for handling environmental differences while maintaining the same artifact.

finalQuestions.prompt: An auditor verifies the correspondence between the artifacts deployed to production and the tests. Select two incorrect actions.
finalQuestions.title: Tracking production artifacts

choices.text: Embed the URL for each environment and rebuild the production artifact.
choices.explanation: Rebuilding creates a difference from the tested artifact.

choices.text: Provide the destination URL as external configuration and deploy the digest tested in the test environment to the next environment.
choices.explanation: This handles environment differences without rebuilding the artifact and keeps the tested and deployed targets identical.

choices.text: Have an operator manually change the production destination each time without keeping a record.
choices.explanation: This loses reproducibility and auditability.

choices.text: Using the “latest” tag means that the tested artifact does not need to be identified.
choices.explanation: The “latest” tag alone cannot fix the exact artifact being deployed.

choices.text: Associate and store the source commit, artifact digest, and test results.
choices.explanation: This is the correct action because it enables tracking of the change, artifact, and tests.

finalQuestions.prompt: You are deploying a web service whose destination URL differs between the test and production environments to the next environment without changing the same artifact. Select two correct actions.
finalQuestions.title: Environment Differences and Promotion

choices.text: It is a stop point that allows progression to the next stage solely because the test was executed, regardless of the result.
choices.explanation: A quality gate evaluates whether the result meets defined conditions, not merely whether the test was executed.

choices.text: It is a stop point that prevents artifacts that do not meet the defined tests and passing criteria from being deployed to the next environment.
choices.explanation: This is the correct role of a quality gate.

choices.text: It is a mechanism that lowers the threshold on the spot when requirements are not met in order to keep the scheduled time.
choices.explanation: Lowering conditions without justification when requirements are not met defeats the purpose of a quality gate.

finalQuestions.prompt: The release operator decides whether to deploy to production based on the results from the test environment. Select one correct description of a quality gate.
finalQuestions.title: Quality Gate Stop Conditions

choices.text: Prioritize the scheduled time, deploy to production, and investigate the cause afterward.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. When the quality gate is not met, stop deployment to the next environment without spreading the impact.

choices.text: Stop deployment to the next environment, maintain the known-good version, and investigate the cause of the failure.
choices.explanation: When the criteria are not met, do not proceed to later stages; preserve the known-good version and the test evidence.

choices.text: Keep the defined conditions unchanged and rerun the same tests after making the correction.
choices.explanation: The correct response is to fix the cause and then verify it under the same quality gate conditions.

finalQuestions.prompt: A required test failed in the test environment, and the error rate also exceeded the quality gate threshold. Select the one action that is incorrect for the release owner.
finalQuestions.title: When the Test Environment Fails to Meet the Passing Criteria

choices.text: Distribute the same tested artifacts to part of production and expand the release scope only when predefined criteria are met.
choices.explanation: Using the same artifacts preserves consistency with the validation. Limiting the release scope makes it less likely that an incident will spread.

choices.text: To release as scheduled, raise the upper limit for the acceptable error rate after the criteria have been exceeded.
choices.explanation: Loosening the stop conditions defined before release to match results during operation cannot sufficiently limit the impact on users.

choices.text: Record the acceptance criteria, the responsible person when a failure occurs, the log storage location, and the rerun procedure in advance.
choices.explanation: The decisions to stop and rerun can follow the same procedure even when the responsible person changes.

choices.text: Delete the failed test logs and the artifacts from the successfully running release before redistributing them.
choices.explanation: This loses the records needed to investigate the cause and the artifacts that could be used for rollback.

choices.text: If the criteria are not met, stop expanding the release scope, fix the cause, and then test again under the same conditions.
choices.explanation: The results can be checked against the same criteria, allowing a decision on whether to proceed again.

finalQuestions.prompt: Operations staff deploy new build artifacts to part of production and expand the release scope while using the same tested artifacts to limit the impact. Select two incorrect approaches to this deployment method.
finalQuestions.title: Operating a gradual rollout

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Learn the workflow of testing changes in small increments and delivering tested artifacts to production gradually.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Explain the purpose of inspecting changes through builds and tests.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Explain the purpose of integrating changes frequently and inspecting them through builds and tests.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Distinguish the process of making validated changes ready for release from the process of automating their deployment to production.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Explain why the same artifacts are used across environments and why the items being validated need to be identifiable.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Decide whether to proceed to the next stage based on test results and operating conditions.

blocks.label: Make small integrations and test them immediately
blocks.text: Continuous integration (CI) is a method in which developers frequently integrate changes into a shared branch and run a build and tests each time. When the scope of a change is small, it is easier to connect a failed test with the change that caused it.

blocks.label: Make small integrations and test them immediately
blocks.text: A build creates, for example, executables or container images for distribution from source code. Tests check whether the change works as specified.

blocks.label: Make small integrations and test them immediately
blocks.text: AWS CodePipeline can connect processes such as source retrieval, builds, tests, approvals, and deployments into a pipeline. The team's requirements determine where to place conditions for moving to the next stage.

steps.label: Make small integrations and test them immediately

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Immediately after the development team integrated a change to the order API, the API integration test failed.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check the failed test's name, input, expected value, and actual response.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Identify the change where the test first failed, and reproduce the cause with a small number of changes.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Apply a fix, rerun the same test, and confirm that the result is as expected.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: The broken process was identified and fixed before the change proceeded to production.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: The executable was created by the build, so the order processing should work normally.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: A successful build indicates that a distributable artifact was created. Tests verify whether order processing works as specified.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Repeat integration and testing in small increments.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Builds and tests have different roles.

blocks.label: Distinguishing continuous delivery from continuous deployment
blocks.text: With continuous delivery, changes are built and put through testing so that they remain ready to be deployed to production at any time. When they are deployed is determined by approvals or business rules.

blocks.label: Distinguishing continuous delivery from continuous deployment
blocks.text: With continuous deployment, changes that pass all required checks are deployed to production without human approval. Automatic monitoring, along with stopping or rolling back when an anomaly is detected, is designed as part of the process.

steps.label: Distinguishing continuous delivery from continuous deployment

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Billing changes are approved by an operations staff member during normal business hours, while changes to static help are automatically released to production once the checks succeed.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Confirm the time periods when changes can be made and the conditions for proceeding to production.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Add an approval stage for changes that require approval, and incorporate the necessary checks for both types of changes.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can operate with the process that verifies the contents separated from the decision to release them to production.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If there is a stage where an operations staff member approves the change, automated testing can be omitted.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Automated tests determine whether a change works according to the specification. Approval confirms the conditions for proceeding to production, such as the scope of impact and the application time.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Distinguish the process of making a release ready from the process of actually deploying it to production.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Define the conditions for proceeding to production according to the type of change.

blocks.label: Deliver the tested artifact to production unchanged
blocks.text: Files for distribution and container images produced by a build are called artifacts. If you rebuild separately for each environment, the dependencies used and the generated files may change, so the contents may differ from those tested.

blocks.label: Deliver the tested artifact to production unchanged
blocks.text: Identify artifacts by build number or digest, and use the same ones in the test environment and in production. Environment-specific values, such as endpoints, are specified in the configuration for the deployment target.

steps.label: Deliver the tested artifact to production unchanged

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: We tested the container image for the order API in the test environment. We will verify the candidate to deploy to production.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Compare the digest from the build result with the digest used in the test environment.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Specify the same digest in the production deployment configuration, and pass the endpoint from the production configuration.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: After deployment, record the digest that is running and the monitoring results.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can verify that what passed testing matches what is running in production.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If you use the same source, building separately for testing and production will produce the same thing.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Artifacts can change because of dependencies and build-time settings. Distribute the same artifact using its verified identifier.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Specify artifacts using information that identifies their contents.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Treat values that depend on the environment where they run as configuration for that environment.

sources.label: AWS CodePipeline input and output artifacts

blocks.label: Decide the conditions for moving to the next stage
blocks.text: A quality gate is a condition used to determine, based on validation results, whether to proceed to the next stage. Before making changes, decide the values used for the decision and the pass criteria, such as the success of required tests, processing time, and error rate.

blocks.label: Decide the conditions for moving to the next stage
blocks.text: Even when starting a rollout with a small number of users, expand the release scope only after obtaining results that meet the conditions. If the conditions are not met, stop the rollout, record the results, and investigate the cause.

steps.label: Decide the conditions for moving to the next stage

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: You will roll out a new version of the order API to a subset of users. You have decided not to expand the release scope if the order error rate exceeds 1%.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check the requests targeted by the new version and the number of errors.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Because the error rate was 2%, stop the rollout.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Record the measurement results and the identifiers of the deployed artifacts, then isolate the cause.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Based on the conditions and evidence, we prevented the scope of the problem from expanding.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Because the tests were run through once, you can proceed to the next stage even if there are failures.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: In addition to running the tests, you must meet the defined pass criteria. If the criteria are not met, investigate the cause before proceeding with the release.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Decide the pass criteria and what to do if a failure occurs in advance.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Record the results and the identifiers of the artifacts.
